slides.title: Title Slide
slides.narration:
Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on
Understanding **Tokens** in **LLMs**.
slides.image_prompt: Title slide: 'Understanding Tokens in LLMs' with a graphic representing AI and text processing.

slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn to
define **tokens**.
You will also explain their importance.
This includes **LLM** context management and cost efficiency.
slides.image_prompt: Learning objectives slide with bullet points: Define tokens, explain importance in LLM context, explain cost efficiency.

slides.title: Pre-requisites
slides.narration:
To follow this tutorial, you should have
a basic understanding of **LLMs**.
You should also know about **prompting**.
slides.image_prompt: Prerequisites slide listing: Basic understanding of LLMs, basic understanding of prompting.

slides.title: What do LLMs Read?
slides.narration:
Have you ever wondered how **LLMs** understand text?
It is not like humans reading words.
Instead, they process something called **tokens**.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration: An LLM brain icon with text flowing in, then breaking into smaller, distinct blocks labeled 'token'.

slides.title: Introducing the Tokenizer
content: A **Tokenizer** is like a special dictionary.
It splits raw text into sub-word pieces.
slides.narration:
So, what creates these **tokens**?
A tool called a **Tokenizer** does this job.
Think of it as a special dictionary.
It breaks down your text into smaller parts.
These are the pieces the **LLM** truly understands.
slides.image_prompt: Graphic: A machine or tool labeled 'Tokenizer' taking a long string of text as input and outputting smaller, distinct blocks (tokens).

slides.title: Token Examples
content: A simple word like "**The**" might be one **token**.
A complex word like "**Tokenization**" might be broken into three **tokens**.
slides.narration:
Let's see some examples.
A common word like "**The**" is often one **token**.
But a longer word like "**Tokenization**" is different.
It might split into multiple **tokens**.
Like "**Token**", then "**iz**", and then "**ation**".
slides.image_prompt: Split screen: Left shows 'The' as one block. Right shows 'Tokenization' breaking into three smaller blocks: 'Token', 'iz', 'ation'.

slides.title: Why should you care?
slides.narration:
So, why is this important for you?
Why should you care about **tokens**?
Knowing about them changes how you work with **LLMs**.
It also impacts how much you pay for them.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration: A person with a thought bubble showing 'tokens', 'cost', and 'context' icons, looking intrigued.

slides.title: Context Windows
content: This window is measured in a fixed number of **tokens**.
slides.narration:
First, let's talk about **Context Windows**.
Think of this as the **LLM**'s short-term memory.
It can only "remember" a certain amount of information.
This limit is set by a fixed number of **tokens**.
For example, it might be 8,192 **tokens**.
slides.image_prompt: Graphic: A brain icon or a memory bar with a number '8,192 tokens' indicating a limit. Text 'Context Window' prominently displayed.

slides.title: Context Window Limits
content: It defines how much "context" you can send.
This includes retrieved documents and your **prompt**.
slides.narration:
This **Context Window** is a hard limit.
It restricts the total information you send.
This includes your **prompt** itself.
It also includes any documents you provide.
All of it must fit within the **token** limit.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration: A funnel with text blocks (representing documents and prompts) going in, and a fixed-size container at the bottom labeled 'Context Window (max tokens)'.

slides.title: API Cost
slides.narration:
Next, consider the cost.
When you use **LLM** services, you pay per **token**.
So, if you use more **tokens**, your cost will be higher.
It's like paying for data usage on your phone.
slides.image_prompt: Graphic: A calculator or bill showing 'cost per token' with an upward arrow for more tokens leading to higher cost.

slides.title: Efficient RAG and Cost Savings
slides.narration:
But you can be smart about it.
An efficient **RAG** system uses fewer **tokens**.
This means it becomes much cheaper to run.
For example, **GraphRAG** reduced **token** usage significantly.
It saved between 26% and 97% of **tokens**.
slides.image_prompt: Infographic: Two bar charts side-by-side. One 'Traditional' with high token count/cost. One 'Efficient RAG' with significantly lower token count/cost.

slides.title: Chunking Documents
content: This means breaking them into smaller parts.
Each part fits within the **Context Window**.
slides.narration:
Finally, let's look at **Chunking**.
When we process large documents, we often "**chunk**" them.
This means splitting them into smaller, manageable pieces.
Each of these pieces must fit into the **LLM**'s **Context Window**.
This helps the **LLM** process information effectively.
slides.image_prompt: Graphic: A large document icon being broken down into several smaller, numbered document pieces, each fitting into a small box representing a context window.

slides.title: Summary
slides.narration:
With this, we come to the end of this tutorial.
Let's summarise.
We learned that **LLMs** process **tokens**, not words.
A **Tokenizer** breaks text into these **tokens**.
Understanding **tokens** is crucial for **LLM** performance.
It affects both **Context Windows** and **API** costs.
slides.image_prompt: Summary slide with key takeaways as bullet points: LLMs use tokens, Tokenizers split text, Tokens impact Context Windows & API costs.

slides.title: Assignment
content: Paste a paragraph of text into it.
See how they are split into **tokens**.
slides.narration:
As an assignment, please do the following.
Find an online **token** counter tool.
Paste a paragraph of text into it.
Observe the number of **tokens** generated.
Now, try different words and phrases.
See how they are split into individual **tokens**.
slides.image_prompt: Assignment slide: A computer screen showing a text box for input and a counter displaying 'X tokens'.
